Odyssey allows to scale processing performance by adding additional worker threads sharing same server pools. Something similar could be achieved in PgBouncer by starting several processes listening same port. Yet they will live their own life and have separate server connections.

It allows to automatically rollback transactions and cancel PostgreSQL backends on client disconnections. Also, it tries to avoid unnecessary parameter settings for reuse, server disconnections and generally optimize io by pipelining requests and replies. Network support optimization in PgBouncer is quite good too.

Odyssey tries to forward real error messages from PostgreSQL when possible. For example, when it cannot connect to server.

It allows to have more settings per pool that can be tweaked explicitly for `database:user:server`. For example: different TLS settings per server, idle times, limits, auth modes, cancel, error forwarding and so on.

It should be much easier with Odyssey to track client errors by id and just grep it or aggregate
its log file. Odyssey allows to configure its log format for easier parsing.

Odyssey partially compatible with PgBouncer console commands. We used it for smoother migration in our monitoring. Currently following PgBouncer commands are supported: `show stats`, `show servers`, `show clients`, `show lists`.  Probably monitoring tools should work and if something is not supported it should not be hard to implement it.

In general SQL feature map for pooling modes should be the same for Odyssey and PgBouncer.

Following stuff is not implemented at the moment: configuration file reload by signal, support for unix sockets, authentication by PAM and HBA.

Odyssey currently runs only on Linux (mostly because of event loop implementation `epoll(7)`). It should be not a problem to add BSD systems support in feature.

Thanks, yes, for me it's the most discouraging problem with standalone postgresql poolers. I'm not quite sure what should the implementation look like. Deallocating and re-preparing everything on server connection reuse seem way too much overhead to me.

Under certain assumptions (prepared statements named based on hashes of the SQL they code; variables like `search_path` or `enable_sort` remain stable) the pooler could somehow track whether a server session has a query prepared and issue PREPARE command on demand only if necessary, and perhaps even DEALLOCATE them if worried about backend memory usage. Even if the assumptions don't hold it'd still be possible to track all that stuff. Maybe it's all too complicated to keep things lightweight and lock-free though -- we'll have to deeper inspect the traffic, and to maintain a global map of prepared statements.

First that comes to mind: when client connects, a pooler needs to setup client with a server configuration parameters. I think we could insert non-PostgreSQL one, something like `odyssey_active` presence of which can tell a client that it is using pooler. In that case, no additional queries will be needed. I wonder will that trick properly work with libpq and other client drivers.

In my experience (having written the original pgjdbc patch to support transaction pooling mode) the benefits of transaction pooling far outweigh any gains from reusing prepared statements.

If you have large planning time you probably can just use session pooling as transaction pooling is usually designed for quick transactions so that the resource can be returned to the pooler as soon as possible.

The engineering effort required to implement this is... large.
If you know which statements you want prepared, there's always the [preprepare](https://github.com/dimitri/preprepare) project.

Odyssey tries to find routes, using following logic:

If exact `database` name is not found, It will try to use `default.user`.
if `database` name is found and no `user` is found, it will try to use `database.default`.
If both `database` and `user` not found, then `default.default` will be used.
If `database` or `user` `default` section are not defined, it will reject the connection attempt.

Hi. Its probably a little bit trickier.

When client connects, its connection accepted from system worker: https://github.com/yandex/odyssey/blob/master/sources/system.c#L65 Then this connection transfered to a next worker from the worker pool.

Worker reads startup packet from client and asks router (which risides in system worker) to match a route for the client: https://github.com/yandex/odyssey/blob/master/sources/frontend.c#L1035

Depending on route type (remote or local) worker handles client requests. In case of console requests (which is local) all query requests are forwarded to console subsystem (which resides in system worker too): https://github.com/yandex/odyssey/blob/master/sources/frontend.c#L495

So basically, all shared data lives in system worker context (several subsystems: router, console, cron). All synchronization between workers is done by using channels and messages. No direct locking is used.

One worker can host thousands of clients and new workers can be added to handle more workload.

Basically overall logic is okey. But there are some issues.

1) Unfortunately this will not work with session pooling, since session pool clients never detach its server: https://github.com/yandex/odyssey/blob/master/sources/frontend.c#L609. To make this work, there are client notification mechanism, which is used to force client to disconnect during config reload or KILL_CLIENT command: https://github.com/yandex/odyssey/blob/master/sources/frontend.c#L665. There are need to be introduced some new client operation that would force to detach from current server. Yet, this might brake session pooling support for PREPARED statements and other stuff. So probably PAUSE/RESUME should be supported with transaction pooling only? If so, we should pick only those servers. I could not find any restriction mention about this in PgBouncer documentation. 

2) od_parser_next() does not allocate memory, so for string tokens token.size must be used everywhere. https://github.com/yandex/odyssey/pull/43/commits/5fa141d49b6463c8424ec8d5d7279a9bb4059943#diff-9313c985cfb35d45dc2da8f7d957cb74R758

3) This sleep should be used carefully, since it will make whole console processing stop because of continuously attempt to sleep for 1 second:
https://github.com/yandex/odyssey/pull/43/commits/5fa141d49b6463c8424ec8d5d7279a9bb4059943#diff-9313c985cfb35d45dc2da8f7d957cb74R799
Probably some other mechanism should be introduced here. Maybe each console_query() should be created inside new coroutine or some other mechanism should be considered, like router attach logic: https://github.com/yandex/odyssey/blob/master/sources/router.c#L298.

4) config_storage must be touched cautiously, since its new version might be created during config reload:
https://github.com/yandex/odyssey/pull/43/commits/766db8d70f5da255fbbe15090ab4fee706a9a525#diff-51cdf03629ff247c67d0dc52deb33ba2R58. There are possible situations when several configuration versions exists and older ones are waiting to be expired. Maybe it would be better to move this state to server object.

Looks like there are a lot of water stones here, I probably should help with it :)

1. I think we should just explicitly support only transactional pooling here, otherwise this will not work for clients who wants session pool guarantees: http://pgbouncer.github.io/features.html (SQL feature map for pooling modes).

3. `machine_sleep()` will switch current coroutine execution context to any other one, which is ready. Console subsystem is driven by single coroutine here: https://github.com/yandex/odyssey/blob/master/sources/console.c#L869. It simply loops https://github.com/yandex/odyssey/blob/master/sources/console.c#L829 and waits for new console requests. We probably could create a new coroutine here: https://github.com/yandex/odyssey/blob/master/sources/console.c#L839 instead of executing the request directly. Coroutine will exit automatically after return from its main function. We should be aware that there are possible situation when several coroutines executing console queries and accessing shared system data. This should be not a problem, pretty much all other subsystems (cron, system, router) are doing the same.

@x4m I just came across this via GSoC, and found it interesting. I can relate to #1 and #2 well.

The features mentioned in the GSoc Ideas List wiki are:

1. Redirecting read query on standby only if standby is lagging no more than X seconds
2. Redirecting read query on standby unless there was recent write (writer should see his writes)
3. Redirecting some read queries on syn or async standby

I'm curious how these would be implemented:
1. *Read if rep. lag <X s*: Does Odyssey already track replication lag of standbys, or will it need to periodically query standbys to compute replication lag using something like `pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()`?

2. *Read-after-writes*: Doesn't this require one to track some 'recent writes' state (i.e. request contexts/ids of recent writes against which subsequent reads can be matched, where 'recent' is defined by a time window)? Currently I see that database+user info is used to match requests to rules. Since recency-of-writes based routing seems to imply some dynamic state, did you have a strategy in mind to implement this that is in line with current architecture of the odyssey library?

3. Could you expand on this a bit? Is it just generally load balancing across read-slaves? Replication lag would be a factor here too, right?

Apologies if these questions are naive - feel free to point me to other resources if I can find answers elsewhere (code, mailing lists, wiki etc.)

Hey, looks like a big pile of work! Thanks for the interest in the project.

Currently Odyssey rely on Machinarium for low-level management which intentionally should include memory management as well. From Machinarium perspective allocated objects (messages for example) are cached and reused after being freed to reduce interactions with system allocator. Since work is done in multi-threaded environment Machinarium keeps message cache associated with each created thread separately to reduce locking and control memory pools usage of malloc. Basically Odyssey tries to avoid system memory allocations and rely on cache when possible.

Machinarium interaction is based around sending and receiving messages. This might be an issue with introduced Postgres style pool allocations. So I am saying, that this approach might not cover all cases. But still can be very convenient in case if we want to introduce some kind of functionality which includes DBMS style processing to Odyssey.

Do you have such plans? :smiley_cat:

Basicaly I was thinking about custom storages. @mkabilov had an idea to use odyssey instead of internal proxy in `stolon` so I made that implementation. When client starts working with odyssey it gets connection information (about current master `postgres` instance) from the storage. Then I thought I need some way to reliably cleanup client related data for the storage (each client has some state) and config related data (each storage will have its config too) so I made these memory contexts.
